title: RC Circuit Charging: The Time Constant τ = RC
hook: When you flip a switch to charge a capacitor through a resistor, the voltage doesn't jump—it climbs exponentially. The speed of that climb is set by the time constant τ = RC. After one τ, the capacitor reaches about 63% of the supply; after five τ, it's essentially full. Adjust R, C, and V0 to see how τ controls the pace.

equation.caption: Capacitor voltage during charging in a series RC circuit.

compute: function compute(inputs){ const R = inputs.R; const C = inputs.C; const V0 = inputs.V0; const tau = R * C; const tMax = 5 * tau; const N = 100; const t = []; const V = []; for (let i = 0; i <= N; i++) { const ti = (i / N) * tMax; t.push(ti); V.push(V0 * (1 - Math.exp(-ti / tau))); } const Vtau = V0 * (1 - Math.exp(-1)); const V5tau = V0 * (1 - Math.exp(-5)); const table = { columns: ['t (s)', 'V(t) (V)'], rows: [] }; for (let i = 0; i <= 10; i++) { const ti = (i / 10) * tMax; const Vi = V0 * (1 - Math.exp(-ti / tau)); table.rows.push([ti.toFixed(4), Vi.toFixed(4)]); } const insight = `At t = τ = ${tau.toFixed(4)} s, V = ${Vtau.toFixed(3)} V (${(100 * (1 - Math.exp(-1))).toFixed(1)}% of V₀). At t = 5τ, V = ${V5tau.toFixed(3)} V (${(100 * (1 - Math.exp(-5))).toFixed(1)}% of V₀).`; return { tau, Vtau, V5tau, series: { x: t, lines: [{ name: 'V(t)', y: V }], marker: { x: tau, y: Vtau } }, table, insight }; }
steps: The time constant is \(\tau = RC\). With \(R = {{R}}\,\Omega\) and \(C = {{C}}\,\mathrm{F}\), \(\tau = {{tau}}\,\mathrm{s}\).
The capacitor voltage follows \(V(t) = V_0\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)\).

explorations.title: Effect of time constant on charging speed
explorations.predict: If you double the resistance R, what happens to the time it takes to reach 63% of V₀?
explorations.observe: The curve rises more slowly. The marker at t = τ moves to the right, and τ doubles to 2 s. The voltage at t = τ is still 0.632 V₀.
explorations.why: Because τ = RC, increasing R increases τ, so the exponent -t/τ becomes less negative for a given t, making the exponential approach slower.

explorations.title: Voltage at one and five time constants
explorations.predict: What fraction of V₀ does the capacitor reach after 5τ?
explorations.why: The factor (1 - e^{-t/τ}) depends only on t/τ. At t = τ it is 1 - e^{-1} ≈ 0.632; at t = 5τ it is 1 - e^{-5} ≈ 0.993.

self_tests.name: Voltage at τ is 63.2% of V0

limitation: This model assumes an ideal capacitor and resistor with no parasitic inductance or resistance, and a step input at t=0. It does not account for dielectric absorption or leakage currents, which can cause the final voltage to deviate slightly from V₀.
misconception: Students often think the capacitor charges linearly or that it reaches full voltage after one time constant. In reality, the charging is exponential and it takes about 5τ to reach 99% of the final value.

claims.text: The time constant τ is the product of resistance and capacitance: τ = RC.
The capacitor voltage during charging is V(t) = V₀(1 - e^{-t/τ}).
After one time constant, the capacitor reaches approximately 63.2% of the supply voltage.
After five time constants, the capacitor is considered fully charged (≈99.3% of V₀).
In our simulation, we assume an ideal step input and neglect parasitic effects, so the computed curve is an idealization.

outcomes.outcome: Explain the meaning of the time constant τ = RC and how it depends on R and C.
Write the charging equation V(t) = V₀(1 - e^{-t/τ}) and identify each symbol.
Calculate the voltage at t = τ and t = 5τ and relate to the 63% and 99% points.
Interpret the charging curve and identify the initial condition V(0) = 0.
